body: We cleaned out the beds, cut a clean edge along the lawn and the walk, and finished them with fresh mulch.

posts.hook: Most of a paver patio is under the pavers.
body: From the top down: pavers with sand swept into the joints, a thin layer of bedding sand, at least 4 inches of compacted stone base, then fabric on firm, compacted soil. An edge restraint keeps the pavers from creeping, and the surface falls away from the house so water runs off.
When pavers sink or shift, the base underneath is usually the reason. The 4-inch minimum comes from the Concrete Masonry and Hardscapes Association's paver guidance.

An edge restraint at every open side
A slope away from the house, so water runs off

posts.hook: Before you cut down a tree in Mount Pleasant, measure it.
body: On a residential lot the Town protects trees 16 inches or more across, measured 4 1/2 feet off the ground, and pines from 24 inches. A short list of species, sweet gum among them, never needs a permit.

The request goes through the Town's online permit system and costs $50. Take a protected tree down without one and the Town fines both the homeowner and whoever cut it. That's why we ask about the permit before anything goes on the calendar.
posts.cta: The full answer, with the Town's own rules, is on our website under Guides.

slides.title: Do you need a permit to cut down a tree in Mount Pleasant?
slides.sub: Usually, yes. Here's how to tell.

slides.title: How to tell
items: Measure across the trunk 4 1/2 feet off the ground

Sweet gum and a few other species never need a permit
The request is $50 through the Town
No permit: the Town fines the owner and the cutter

posts.hook: If water sits against your house after it rains, check which way the ground slopes.
body: Building code asks for the ground to fall at least 6 inches in the first 10 feet away from a house (International Residential Code, R401.3). When it slopes toward the house instead, rainwater runs back to the foundation.
The fix is regrading: cut the high side, fill and pack the low side, and leave the finished grade falling away from the house.
posts.cta: Not sure which way yours runs? Text us a photo after the next rain: (843) 998-5593.

posts.hook: Does your yard hold water for days after a storm?
body: Usually it's the grade. The ground holds water in a low spot or sends it toward the house, and the Lowcountry's high water table leaves it nowhere to soak in.
Where there's enough fall, we regrade. Where there isn't, a swale or a French drain carries the water to somewhere it's allowed to go.

posts.hook: Fall is the best season to plant shrubs here. Here's how deep they should go.
body: Clemson Extension's rules: dig the hole two to five times wider than the root ball but no deeper, set the top roots level with the ground or slightly above it, backfill with the soil that came out, and finish with 2 to 3 inches of mulch kept off the stems (HGIC 1052).
Planted in fall, a shrub has the whole cool season to grow roots before summer heat.

posts.hook: Grind the stump or pull it out? It depends on what goes there next.
body: Grind it if the spot will be lawn or a bed. Grinding takes the stump below the surface and leaves the roots to rot.
Pull it if anything will be built or dug there. The excavator lifts the stump and root ball out whole, and the hole is backfilled and packed.

alternates.hook: Thinking about new sod? In Charleston, timing matters.
body: Clemson Extension says sod is best laid in mid to late spring or in the fall, early enough to root before cold weather. Which grass comes down to sun: St. Augustine takes the most shade but still needs 4 to 6 hours of direct sun, zoysia does well in sun or part shade, centipede is the low-upkeep choice for open sun away from salt, and Bermuda needs full sun.
alternates.cta: Planning a new lawn for spring? Text (843) 998-5593.

slides.title: When should sod go down in Charleston?
slides.sub: Mid to late spring, or early fall.
slides.alt: When should sod go down in Charleston? Mid to late spring, or early fall.

items: St. Augustine: most shade, still needs 4 to 6 hours of sun
Zoysia: sun or part shade
Centipede: low upkeep, open sun, away from salt
Bermuda: full sun only
